- TCP is a connection-oriented transport protocol.
- UDP is a connectionless transport protocol.
- TCP uses a three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
- IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long.
- IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long.
- HTTP defaults to port 80.
- HTTPS defaults to port 443.
- SSH defaults to port 22.
- DNS mainly uses port 53.
- DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.
- An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address.
- An AAAA record maps a name to an IPv6 address.
- A CNAME record aliases one name to another.
- An MX record names a domain's mail servers.
- DHCP assigns IP addresses automatically.
- ARP maps IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses.
- IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery instead of ARP.
- A MAC address is 48 bits long.
- The OSI model has seven layers.
- The TCP/IP model usually has four layers.
- Routers forward packets between networks.
- Switches forward frames within a LAN.
- Hubs repeat signals to every port.
- NAT translates private addresses to public ones.
- 10.0.0.0/8 is a private IPv4 range.
- 172.16.0.0/12 is a private IPv4 range.
- 192.168.0.0/16 is a private IPv4 range.
- 127.0.0.1 is the IPv4 loopback address.
- ::1 is the IPv6 loopback address.
- CIDR notation writes the prefix length after a slash.
- A /24 IPv4 subnet holds 256 addresses.
- TTL limits how many hops a packet can make.
- ICMP carries error and diagnostic messages.
- Ping uses ICMP echo request and reply.
- Traceroute reveals the hops along a path.
- BGP routes traffic between autonomous systems.
- OSPF is a link-state interior routing protocol.
- RIP is a distance-vector routing protocol.
- RIP limits routes to 15 hops.
- Ethernet's standard MTU is 1500 bytes.
- Jumbo frames often carry a 9000-byte MTU.
- TCP's MSS is usually MTU minus 40 bytes.
- VLANs split one switch into logical networks.
- 802.1Q is the VLAN tagging standard.
- Wi-Fi is defined by the IEEE 802.11 family.
- WPA3 is the newest Wi-Fi security standard.
- TLS encrypts traffic for HTTPS.
- TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for a full handshake.
- QUIC runs over UDP.
- HTTP/3 is built on QUIC.
- HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one connection.
- Latency is the delay for data to travel.
- Bandwidth is the maximum data rate of a link.
- Throughput is the data rate actually achieved.
- Jitter is variation in packet delay.
- Packet loss forces TCP retransmissions.
- TCP congestion control adjusts the send rate.
- CUBIC is Linux's default TCP congestion algorithm.
- BBR models bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip time.
- A firewall filters traffic by rules.
- Stateful firewalls track connection state.
- A VPN tunnels traffic over an encrypted link.
- WireGuard is a lightweight modern VPN protocol.
- A proxy forwards requests for clients.
- A reverse proxy sits in front of servers.
- Load balancers spread traffic across servers.
- CDNs cache content close to users.
- Anycast shares one IP across many locations.
- Multicast sends one stream to many receivers.
- Broadcast reaches every host on a segment.
- Ports range from 0 to 65535.
- Ports below 1024 are well-known ports.
- Ephemeral ports serve the client side of connections.
- A socket is an IP address plus a port.
- SMTP sends email, commonly on port 25 or 587.
- IMAP retrieves email, commonly on port 993 with TLS.
- NTP synchronizes clocks over UDP port 123.
- SNMP monitors network devices.
- Fiber optics carry data as light.
- Cat6 cable supports 10 Gbps over short runs.
